title: Adapting complex concepts to different audiences: from Gaussian Process intuition to formalism
text:
Challenges


Hierarchical Gaussian Process regression is a highly abstract statistical framework that can be intimidating even for quantitatively trained scientists. Yet, using GPMelt effectively requires understanding several interconnected concepts spanning multiple levels of abstraction, from the intuition behind Gaussian Process regression and its application to Thermal Proteome Profiling data, to the way biological experimental designs are represented within a hierarchical statistical model.
The communication challenge was therefore twofold: lowering the barrier created by mathematical complexity while preserving the concepts necessary for meaningful use of the method. At the same time, the resources had to work for audiences ranging from experimental biologists with limited statistical training to bioinformaticians and statisticians with very different levels of familiarity with Gaussian Processes.
The key challenge was to communicate the same underlying ideas across multiple levels of abstraction and audiences without sacrificing clarity, rigor, or engagement.





Approach


Rather than introducing the framework through mathematical formalism, I designed a series of short, visual-first videos that introduced the key concepts progressively, from intuitive explanations aimed at a broad audience to more advanced material for statistically trained users. The goal was not only to make the principles easier to understand, but to provide multiple entry points into the same underlying concepts.
Key design choices included:

prioritising conceptual understanding before introducing formal definitions;
adapting vocabulary, examples, and level of detail to each audience;
using visual metaphors, colour coding, and animation to make abstract concepts more tangible;
progressively increasing the level of abstraction, from intuitive explanations to more formal statistical reasoning.





Strengths



Adapting explanations to audiences with different levels of expertise;
Making complex concepts accessible without oversimplification;
Communicating across multiple levels of abstraction while preserving rigor;
Translation between disciplines and domains (e.g. from biological data to mathematical modelling; from statistical analysis to biological interpretation);
Connecting experimental, statistical, and computational perspectives;
Designing learning pathways that support progressive understanding, from intuition to formalization;
Creating high-quality visual explanations of abstract concepts (figures, animation, storytelling);
Developing concise, engaging educational content for self-directed learning.






Impact


These resources were designed to help users understand the reasoning behind the model, not only to learn how to use GPMelt in practice. By making the underlying statistical framework more approachable across different levels of expertise, they aimed to reduce the gap between method developers and end users.
This allows users to engage with the modelling framework at a depth appropriate to their needs and expertise, while maintaining a coherent conceptual link between the biological experiment and its statistical analysis. As a result, researchers can engage more confidently with the methodology, better understand its assumptions and limitations, and use the resulting analyses more critically and effectively.
Ultimately, the objective was to transform the model from a black box into a tool that users could meaningfully understand and build upon. By focusing on the underlying modelling principles rather than software usage alone, these resources provide a foundation for adapting and extending the framework to new experimental settings and data types.




Explore the videos and see how the communication strategy comes to life

title: Scientific storytelling: Designing a high-impact conference poster
text:
Challenges


At large international conferences, poster sessions are highly competitive environments in which hundreds of projects compete simultaneously for attention. Standing out from the crowd is therefore essential to attract an audience before they move on to the next poster, often leaving only a few minutes to pitch the project.
For GPMelt, this challenge was amplified by the nature of the project itself. Advanced statistical methodologies can appear intimidating to researchers unfamiliar with sophisticated modelling approaches, creating a barrier not only to understanding the work, but even to initially approaching the poster and engaging with the presenter.
The challenge was therefore to create a poster that attracted attention, lowered this initial barrier, and encouraged researchers from diverse backgrounds to engage confidently with both the project and the person presenting it.

title: Visual thinking for scientific communication:  Designing visuals for clarity and engagement
text:
Challenges


The common challenge across these visuals is to translate complex concepts into intuitive visual representations without sacrificing scientific accuracy. Many of the ideas involved are abstract, interdisciplinary, or highly technical, making them difficult to communicate effectively through text alone.
Regardless of their communicative purpose, each visual therefore requires balancing multiple objectives simultaneously: accessibility for non-specialists, sufficient depth for expert audiences, clarity to support understanding and engagement, and enough visual appeal to attract and maintain attention.
The challenge is not simply to illustrate information, but to identify the visual representation that best supports understanding, highlights the key message, and communicates effectively across different backgrounds and communication contexts.





Approach


I design visuals as communication tools rather than decorative illustrations. The objective is not simply to represent information, but to support understanding through visual reasoning and synthesis.
Key principles:

simplifying complex ideas without losing their essential meaning;
combining abstract concepts with concrete visual representations to support intuition and understanding;
synthesising information from multiple disciplines or sources into coherent visual narratives;
using visual hierarchy, colour, and layout to guide attention towards the most important information;
adapting the style and level of detail to the intended audience and communication objective.





Strengths



Bridging audiences with different backgrounds through visual communication;
Distilling complex ideas into their essential communicable elements;
Condensing large amounts of information into clear visual summaries;
Designing visuals that support curiosity, reasoning, understanding, and decision-making;
Adapting visual communication across different stages of the communication process.






Impacts


Some concepts are difficult to communicate effectively through text, formulas, or verbal explanations alone, yet become immediately more accessible once visualised. By transforming abstract ideas into intuitive visual representations, these illustrations supported conceptual abstraction, knowledge translation, and information synthesis across a wide range of communication contexts.
These visual representations also provided a common language between disciplines. By translating abstract concepts, workflows, and analytical reasoning into intuitive visual forms, they facilitated discussions between researchers with different areas of expertise and helped communicate key ideas more efficiently.
More broadly, this work reinforced the idea that effective visuals are not merely decorative elements. When carefully designed, they can reduce the intimidation often associated with theoretical or highly technical content, making complex ideas more approachable while preserving their depth and meaning.

title: Communicating potential, not just results:  Persuasive scientific storytelling in a 10-minute conference talk
text:
Challenges


The talk targeted a diverse audience ranging from experimental biologists to computational researchers, most of whom were not specialists in Thermal Proteome Profiling.
The challenge was not only to explain the core idea clearly and accurately, but also to do so within a ten-minute conference format. This left very little time to introduce the scientific problem, explain the proposed solution, and persuade the audience that the idea mattered.
The communication challenge was further complicated by the structure of the message itself. The talk began with a highly specialised methodological problem before gradually revealing a broader question hidden beneath it: how reducing experimental costs could contribute to making advanced scientific methodologies more accessible. The key challenge was therefore to guide the audience from a niche technical concept to its wider implications without losing either scientific rigour or narrative momentum.

Using comparative visualisation (bar charts, boxplots, violin plots, and statistical significance tests) to compare two analytical approaches. Together, these representations highlight differences in the phosphosites detected by each method and show that phosphosites uniquely identified by GPMelt are associated with higher functional scores, supporting their biological relevance (Figure 6.9BC from [1]). (© 2025 Cécile Le Sueur)


Comparing model fits produced by NPARC (top row) and GPMelt (bottom row). While NPARC provides only a fitted curve, GPMelt additionally communicates uncertainty through a 95% confidence region around the posterior mean estimate, supporting more informed interpretation of the results (Figure 6.8D from [1]). (© 2025 Cécile Le Sueur)


Using multidimensional scaling (MDS) to evaluate the effectiveness of three batch-correction strategies. By projecting complex longitudinal data into an interpretable visual space, the figure reveals which method successfully aligns measurements across temperatures, conditions, and replicates (Figure B20 from [1]). (© 2025 Cécile Le Sueur)


Using ROC curves to compare the performance of four statistical methods across two datasets. The visualisation revealed the consistently poorer performance of one approach, motivating further investigation and ultimately leading to the identification of its sensitivity to outliers (Figure 6.6 from [1]). (© 2025 Cécile Le Sueur)


Comparing real and permuted datasets through volcano plots. The unexpected presence of numerous discoveries in the permuted datasets (second row) revealed a previously unnoticed batch effect, illustrating how visualisation can uncover hidden patterns and guide methodological investigation (Figure 7.7 from [1]). (© 2025 Cécile Le Sueur)


Using p-value histograms to diagnose a statistical calibration problem. The visualisation immediately revealed that the method produced miscalibrated p-values on this dataset (left panel), leading to the discovery that non-sigmoidal data violated the model assumptions. Removing these data restored calibration (right panel) and confirmed the source of the issue.(Figure 6.8C from [1]). (© 2025 Cécile Le Sueur)


Combining conceptual illustration (A) and model diagnostics (B) to explain convergence analysis. The figure uses a simplified optimisation landscape (A) to visualise how model fitting can become trapped in local optima before reaching a better solution (as examplified in the second panel in (B)), helping make an abstract statistical concept more intuitive (Figure 5.3 from [1]). (© 2025 Cécile Le Sueur)

title: Striking image for GPMelt
text:
Click on the image to zoom in! (© 2024 Cécile Le Sueur)




This image captures the transformative power of GPMelt to fully explore the complexity of melting curve behavior.
The mosaic of non-sigmoidal curves in the background symbolizes the diverse range of melting profiles that GPMelt can integrate. Unlike state-of-the-art methods, GPMelt is agnostic to curve shape, breaking free from the constraints of sigmoidal melting behavior. Every curve — no matter how irregular — finds a place in the analysis, allowing for a more inclusive understanding of the thermal proteome.
Illuminated by the X-ray viewer, two non-sigmoidal curves emerge from the shadows. No longer obscured or discarded, they become fully accessible and visible, ready for interpretation. GPMelt brings these previously overlooked curves into the spotlight, making them a valuable part of the TPP-TR dataset. This comprehensive vision transforms our capacity to analyze protein thermal stability, opening up new possibilities for discovery.
The stethoscope, lit by the X-ray viewer’s glow, serves as a metaphor for GPMelt’s diagnostic power. It symbolizes the newfound ability of users to uncover and diagnose these unconventional curves. GPMelt doesn’t just detect atypical melting behaviors; it empowers users to explore the underlying biology, leading them toward novel discoveries. By fitting all curve types, including the most complex, GPMelt opens the door to advanced analyses like clustering, which could inspire hypotheses about the origins of non-sigmoidality and reveal deeper biological insights.
In essence, GPMelt is not just a tool; it’s a breakthrough that exposes previously hidden part of the meltome, pushing the boundaries of thermal proteome profiling and giving access to biological phenomena that were previously out of reach.

title: Building intuition for statistical reasoning:  Multiple testing, False Discovery Rate (FDR) and p-values miscalibration
text:
Challenges


Modern biological experiments increasingly rely on high-throughput technologies that generate large datasets and create opportunities to test hundreds or thousands of hypotheses simultaneously. While this offers considerable scientific potential, it also introduces new statistical challenges that require additional caution during data analysis.
Multiple testing, False Discovery Rate (FDR) control, and p-value calibration are therefore central concepts in modern biological research, yet many researchers struggle to develop an intuitive understanding of what they mean in practice. Although encountered routinely, the reasoning behind them is often perceived as abstract, mathematically complex, or inaccessible.
The communication challenge was compounded by the highly heterogeneous statistical backgrounds of the workshop’s participants, ranging from researchers with minimal formal training in statistics to others with substantial quantitative experience.
Another challenge was therefore not simply to explain statistical procedures, but to help participants build intuition and confidence, understand what changes when moving from single to multiple hypothesis testing, and develop the reasoning needed to engage with these concepts independently after the session.

title: Building intuition for statistical reasoning:  Multiple testing, False Discovery Rate (FDR) and p-values miscalibration
